_about: The law hub (plan 7.6f, third round). The card is named 'instruction' on the site and its id is 'law'. The words are the Hebrew noun תּוֹרָה (Torah) and the Greek noun νόμος, which the Greek Old Testament uses for it (187 of its 220 uses are rendered νόμος there) and the New Testament uses for the law of Moses and for the other 'laws' it names. The hub never says they are one word: every verse names the word it stands on. תּוֹרָה is 'law' and also 'instruction' and 'teaching' (a father's, a mother's, a priest's, God's), so the rows stand on the law sense (MACULA's gloss 'law') and the instruction sense is its own row, 'Instruction and teaching', listed by hand from the glosses 'instruction', 'teaching' and 'ruling'. The Torah is first heard on its own terms (the law of the LORD, given through Moses, the book of the law, kept, loved, forsaken, read aloud, taught, written on the heart, for the foreigner, the offerings and uncleanness), then the New Testament's sayings (the Law and the Prophets, faith, works, grace, under the law, sin and the curse, the other 'laws' it names) and then the contested block. The contested point -- the law and the Christian (fulfilled, ended, or continuing as a guide) -- is shown in three rows set side by side in the alphabetical order of their labels, each with the same no-side sentence; the page names no scheme (no law-and-gospel, no 'third use', no dispensation). Rows as in love.json, righteousness.json, covenant.json and salvation.json: a verse sits in every row it fits (match: all); rows made 'by hand' use 'add', which keeps a verse only where the word really stands in it, so a mistyped reference falls out instead of showing a verse without the word. Built by tools/concepts/hub_build.py into out/concept-hubs/law.json.

titles.noun: What the text says of the law

_words_why: תּוֹרָה (220 verses by the card; the Hebrew) and νόμος (194; the Greek), together because the Greek Old Testament renders the one by the other and the New Testament quotes it so (Heb 8:10 quotes Jer 31:33), but the hub never says they are one word: the Hebrew is 'teaching, instruction, direction' as well as 'law'; the Greek is 'law', and also 'principle' where the Berean prints it so (Rom 3:27, 7:21; see sense_keep). Left out of the words as different: מִצְוָה and ἐντολή (commandment), חֹק and חֻקָּה (statute), מִשְׁפָּט (ordinance, justice), עֵדוּת (testimony), פִּקּוּד (precept), which stand beside the law in a row of their own and have their own cards; and the Aramaic דָּת, a Persian loanword for the king's edict that Ezra 7:12 uses of 'the law of the God of heaven', which is named under the other words. νομικός, νομοδιδάσκαλος, νομοθεσία and ἄνομος are other words of the family and are not counted.
_sense_why: A gloss rule, because תּוֹרָה is two senses in one word: MACULA glosses it 'law' or 'laws' where it is the law and 'instruction', 'teaching' or 'ruling' where it is a parent's teaching (Prov 1:8, 3:1, 4:2, 6:20, 7:2, 13:14, 31:26), a priest's (Mal 2:6-9, Ezek 7:26, Hag 2:11), a prophet's (Isa 1:10, 8:16, 30:9) or God's 'instructions' (Exod 16:4, 16:28). The brief asks that this sense be kept apart: those verses are not in the law rows and are in 'Instruction and teaching' by hand. The Berean does not always follow MACULA's gloss (it prints 'the law' at Isa 8:20 and Jer 18:18 where MACULA says 'teaching' and 'instruction'); the row's note says so, and the page does not choose between the renderings. Isa 2:3 is kept in the law sense (sense_keep): it is the same sentence as Mic 4:2, which MACULA glosses 'law', and the Berean prints 'law' in both.

sense_keep.Isa.2.3: the same sentence as Mic 4:2 ('the law will go forth from Zion'); MACULA glosses it 'instruction' here and 'law' there, and the Berean prints 'law' in both
sense_keep.Rom.3.27: MACULA glosses νόμος 'principle' in 'a law of faith'; the Berean prints 'the law of faith'
sense_keep.Rom.7.21: MACULA glosses νόμος 'principle'; the Berean prints 'I find this law at work'

others._why: Different words the English also renders law, instruction or teaching, named apart with their verses and never handed over as the same word. The Aramaic and Hebrew דָּת are added by hand with their notes (the first verses are the ones a reader would look for). Excluded after the first build: διδάσκω 'teach' (50 verses), διδαχή (29) and διδασκαλία (17), the New Testament's words for teaching, which the English prints beside the Torah's 'instruction' but which say nothing of the law. Left in: מוּסָר 'instruction, discipline' (Proverbs, beside the parents' תּוֹרָה), νομοδιδάσκαλος 'teacher of the law', ἔννομος (1 Cor 9:21, 'under the law of Christ') and the other words with 'law' in them.
others.title: Other words translated “law”, “instruction”, “teaching”

h1882.note: The Aramaic דָּת, a Persian loanword, is the king's edict or decree (Dan 6:8, 6:15, 'the law of the Medes and Persians'). In Ezra 7:12, 7:14, 7:21 and 7:26 it is also 'the law of your God', of the God of heaven. It is a different word from תּוֹרָה, and the page does not make the two one.

h1881.note: The Hebrew דָּת, the same Persian loanword, is the king's edict, custom or law in Esther (1:8, 1:13, 3:8, 4:11). It is a different word from תּוֹרָה, and the page does not make the two one.

h4941.note: The Hebrew מִשְׁפָּט is “justice”, “ordinance” and “judgment” as well as “law”: the Berean prints “standard of law” in Lev 24:22 and “justice” in Prov 1:3 and Hab 1:4. It is a different word from תּוֹרָה, and the page does not make the two one.

_own_words_why: One from each side of what the page keeps apart or sets side by side: the law as perfect (Ps 19:7), the same Hebrew word as a mother's teaching (Prov 1:8), the law going out to the nations (Isa 2:3), 'not to abolish but to fulfill' (Matt 5:17) beside 'Christ is the end of the law' (Rom 10:4), the law as holy (Rom 7:12), the law as guardian (Gal 3:24) and the whole law (Jas 2:10).

Acts.13.38.why: the Greek's 13:38 ends 'from all which you could not be justified by the law of Moses'; the Berean prints those words in 13:39, so 13:38 as shown has no 'law' (as on the righteousness hub)

rows.label: The law of the LORD, of God

not_verses.Luke.2.22: the Berean has 'the Law of Moses' here; 'the Law of the Lord' is the clause that begins in 2:22 and is printed in 2:23 and 2:24

rows.note: The text's own phrase, kept as written: “the Law of the LORD” (Ps 1:2; 19:7), “the Law of the Lord” (Luke 2:23), “God's law” (Rom 7:22; 8:7). The page says nothing of how this law stands to any other.
rows._why: the very next word either side is the LORD, God or Lord (the divine persons by hand: the text itself names Him). Jesus is not in this set: 'the law of Christ' (Gal 6:2) is by hand, under 'Other laws the text names'.

rows.label: Given and set before the people; “the Law of Moses”
rows.note: Several of these verses say “you” or “us”, not Moses by name: Deut 4:8 and 33:4 stand in Moses' speeches, Acts 7:53 is Stephen's (“you who received the law ordained by angels”) and Gal 3:19 says of the law “It was administered through angels by a mediator.” How the law given at Sinai stands to the law now is what the three rows after “Other laws” set side by side, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: Moses named in the verse (מֹשֶׁה, Μωϋσῆς) and, by hand, the verses that say the law was given, set before the people or received (Deut 4:44 'This is the law that Moses set before the Israelites', 33:4, Acts 7:53, Gal 3:19, Heb 9:19). Guarded by the word: each is kept only where תּוֹרָה or νόμος really stands in it.

rows.label: The book of the law; what is written in the law
rows._why: the book (סֵפֶר, βιβλίον) next to the law ('the Book of the Law', Deut 28:61, Josh 8:34, 2 Kgs 22:8, Gal 3:10) and, by hand, the verses that say a thing is 'written in the Law' (2 Kgs 14:6, Neh 10:34, Luke 2:23, John 10:34).

rows.label: The Law and the Prophets
rows.note: In the Gospels and Acts the words are “the Law and the Prophets” (Matt 5:17, 7:12; Acts 13:15). The Old Testament verses here name the law and the prophets side by side, as what the LORD sent and the people refused, and not as a fixed phrase: “the entire Law that I commanded your fathers and delivered to you through My servants the prophets” (2 Kgs 17:13), “would not listen to the law or to the words that the LORD of Hosts had sent by His Spirit through the earlier prophets” (Zech 7:12), “Her prophets are reckless, faithless men. Her priests profane the sanctuary; they do violence to the law” (Zeph 3:4).
rows._why: the word for prophet in the verse with the law: 'the Law and the Prophets' (Matt 5:17, 7:12, 22:40, Luke 16:16, Acts 13:15, 24:14, Rom 3:21), and the Old Testament verses that name the law and the prophets together (2 Kgs 17:13, Neh 9:26, Dan 9:10, Zech 7:12).

rows.label: Keep, do, walk in, obey the law; “I do not forget Your law”
rows.note: The text's own verbs: “keep” (Hebrew שָׁמַר, 'guard, observe'; Gen 26:5), “do”, “walk in” (Ps 119:1), “obey”, and the psalmist's “I do not forget Your law” (Ps 119:61, 109; “I have not forgotten Your law”, 119:153). The same Hebrew word is “the LORD's instruction” in “children unwilling to obey the LORD's instruction” (Isa 30:9) and “instructions” in “whether or not they will follow My instructions” (Exod 16:4); those verses are listed in “Instruction and teaching…” below. The verses that say who can keep it, and what keeping earns, are here and in “The law, and works” and “Sin, trespass, the curse”; the page takes no side.
rows._why: the law as the object of the verbs for keep, do, observe, guard, walk, from the frames (שָׁמַע 'hear' was in the first build and is out: Neh 13:3 'As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded ...' says hear, not obey), with the verses the frames lack added by hand (Gen 26:5 'My laws', the 'walk in' verses, and the New Testament sayings with the verb in another form or in the participle: Rom 2:13 'doers of the law', Gal 3:10 'continue to do', 5:3 'obligated to keep the whole law'). Rule 1: the verb of each is in the verse.

rows.label: Loved and delighted in; called perfect, good, holy, spiritual, true; more precious than gold
rows.note: The text's own words: “his delight is in the Law of the LORD” (Ps 1:2), “The Law of the LORD is perfect” (Ps 19:7), “Oh, how I love Your law!” (Ps 119:97), “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (Rom 7:12), “in my inner being I delight in God's law” (Rom 7:22). “The law is good, if one uses it legitimately” (1 Tim 1:8) is here with them; what the legitimate use is, readers take differently, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that say the law is loved, a delight, perfect, good, holy, true or better than gold. Ps 119 has the word in thirty verses; those that only say 'keep' or 'forsake' are in the rows for keeping and forsaking.

rows.label: Forsaken, rejected, forgotten, transgressed, not kept

not_verses.Ps.119.61: the psalmist says 'I do not forget Your law': the verb is negated, so the verse is in “Keep, do, walk in, obey the law”
not_verses.Ps.119.109: 'I do not forget Your law': negated, in “Keep, do, walk in, obey the law”
not_verses.Ps.119.153: 'I have not forgotten Your law': negated, in “Keep, do, walk in, obey the law”

rows.note: The same Hebrew word, תּוֹרָה, is rejected or treated lightly in verses that stand in “Instruction and teaching…” below, where the Berean prints “instruction” or “law”: “they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts” (Isa 5:24), “Though I wrote for them the great things of My law, they regarded them as something strange” (Hos 8:12), “but have shown partiality in matters of the law” (Mal 2:9). They are listed there by MACULA's gloss of the word, and the page does not say which English is right.
rows._why: the law as the object of forsake, reject, forget, despise, break, transgress, from the frames, with the verses the frames lack added by hand (the passives and the nouns 'a transgressor of the law', Rom 2:25, 2:27, Jas 2:11; the plural 'laws' of Isa 24:5, Dan 9:10).

rows.label: Taught and read aloud; the priests, Levites, scribes and Pharisees

not_verses.Jer.32.23: קָרָא here is 'come upon' (the disaster 'came upon them'), not 'call' or 'read'
not_verses.Jer.44.23: קָרָא here is 'befall' (this disaster has befallen you), not 'call' or 'read'
not_verses.Matt.23.23: Jesus speaking to the scribes and Pharisees of the law's weightier matters: it is Jesus speaking of the law, so it stands in “Jesus speaks of the law”, where it is picked by hand (review, 2026-10-25)

rows.note: The text's own words: “you are to read this law in the hearing of all Israel” (Deut 31:11), “they read from the Book of the Law of God, explaining it and giving insight” (Neh 8:8), “Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to practice it, and to teach its statutes and ordinances in Israel” (Ezra 7:10). The row also holds the verses that name the priests, the Levites, the scribes and the Pharisees beside the law, among them “The Levites ... instructed the people in the Law” (Neh 8:7) and “as to the law, a Pharisee” (Phil 3:5).
rows._why: the words for reading, teaching, priest, Levite, scribe and Pharisee in the verse, from the word-by-word text, with the verses of Deut 17, 31, 33, Ezra 7 and Neh 8 and the New Testament teachers added by hand. A large row on purpose: the law is, in the text, a thing read out and taught; the verbs for 'call' and 'learn' (קָרָא, לָמַד) also stand in verses that only call or learn, which the 16-verse check reads.

rows.label: On the heart, in the mind; “within my heart”
rows.note: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jer 31:33; quoted in Heb 8:10 and 10:16), “the work of the law is written on their hearts” (Rom 2:15), “the law of his God is in his heart” (Ps 37:31). Where Christian traditions part on how these stand to the new covenant and to whom they are said, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand, after a first build: a rule on 'heart' in the verse took Deut 30:10, 2 Kgs 23:25 and Ezra 7:10, where the heart is turning to the LORD or setting itself to study and the law is in a book. Only the verses that say the law is put in, or is in, the heart or mind are kept: Ps 37:31, 40:8, Isa 51:7 ('who have My law in their hearts'), Jer 31:33 and Heb 8:10, 10:16, Rom 2:15, 7:23 and 7:25 ('the law of my mind', 'with my mind I serve the law of God').

rows.label: The foreigner, the Gentiles, the nations; circumcision and uncircumcision

not_verses.Lam.2.9: the nations are where the king and princes are exiled; the verse says 'the law is no more' but nothing of the law and the nations

rows.note: The text's own words: “The same law shall apply to both the native and the foreigner who resides among you” (Exod 12:49), “the law will go forth from Zion” to many peoples (Isa 2:3; Mic 4:2), “the Gentiles, who do not have the law” (Rom 2:14). Where Christian traditions part on how the law stands to Gentile believers, the page takes no side.
rows._why: the foreigner, the Gentiles, the nations or circumcision in the verse; the Old Testament verses that send the law out to the nations or give it to the foreigner too are added by hand (Isa 42:4 'the islands await His instruction' is the Berean's rendering of תּוֹרָה, and MACULA's gloss there is 'law').

rows.label: Instruction and teaching: a father's, a mother's, a priest's, the wise's, God's
rows.note: The same Hebrew word, תּוֹרָה, that the other rows give as “law”. MACULA glosses it “instruction”, “teaching” or “ruling” in these verses and the Berean prints those words in most (Prov 1:8, 13:14, 31:26; Isa 1:10, 30:9; Mal 2:7), and “law” in a few (Isa 8:16, 8:20; Jer 18:18; Hos 8:12; Mal 2:9), “ruling” in Hag 2:11 and “custom” in 2 Sam 7:19. The page does not say the Hebrew has two words: it is one word that is both, and a reader of Proverbs hears “my son, do not forget my teaching” (Prov 3:1) in the same word as “the law of the LORD”. Where the verse is a parent's, it is a parent's; where it is God's, it is God's. The line between this row and the law rows is MACULA's gloss of the word, not a division the Hebrew makes: where the Berean prints “law” (Isa 8:16, 8:20; Jer 18:18; Hos 8:12; Mal 2:9) the verse is here by that gloss, and the page does not say which English is right. In 2 Sam 7:19 the Berean prints “Is this Your custom with man, O Lord GOD?” for the Hebrew phrase תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם (MACULA: “instruction”); the phrase is hard, the verse stands here by the Hebrew word, and the page does not settle what it means.
rows._why: by hand, on the brief's rule that this sense is kept apart by `sense`: every verse where MACULA glosses תּוֹרָה 'instruction', 'teaching', 'instructions' or 'ruling', from the word card (Exod 16:4, 16:28; 2 Sam 7:19; Job 22:22; Ps 78:1; Prov 1:8, 3:1, 4:2, 6:20, 6:23, 7:2, 13:14, 31:26; Isa 1:10, 5:24, 8:16, 8:20, 30:9; Jer 18:18; Ezek 7:26; Hos 8:12; Hag 2:11; Mal 2:6-9). Isa 2:3 is the same gloss and stands in 'The foreigner, the Gentiles, the nations' because it is the sentence of Mic 4:2. 2 Sam 7:19's Berean text is 'Is this Your custom with man?'; the Hebrew תּוֹרַת הָאָדָם is kept here and the row's note says the Berean varies.

rows.label: “This is the law of ...”: the offerings, clean and unclean, childbirth, jealousy, the Nazirite
rows.note: The law of the burnt offering, the grain offering, the guilt offering, the fellowship offering, regarding skin diseases and mildew (the Berean's words for the Hebrew that older translations call leprosy), for a woman giving birth, of jealousy, of the Nazirite, the red heifer, animals and birds that are clean or unclean: the law as a particular ruling for a particular case, in the text's own phrase “This is the law of ...”. The Berean prints “law” for the one word. What the New Testament says of the law as a whole is set out in the three rows below, after “Other laws”, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses of Leviticus and Numbers that say 'This is the law of ...' (the Hebrew chapter numbering of Leviticus 5-6 and Numbers 16-17 differs from the English; ids are the Berean's), with the three verses of Ezekiel's temple that call the temple's ordinances 'laws'. Each is kept only where תּוֹרָה stands.

rows.label: Judged by the law; brought to court

not_verses.Matt.23.23: κρίσις here is 'justice' (justice, mercy and faithfulness), not a judgment under the law
not_verses.Rom.2.15: κατηγορέω here is the thoughts 'accusing or defending' within a person, not a court
not_verses.Rom.8.3: κατακρίνω here is God condemning sin in the flesh, not a judgment by the law

rows.note: The text's own words: “You take Him and judge Him by your own law,” Pilate told them. “We are not permitted to execute anyone,” the Jews replied (John 18:31), “according to that law He must die” (John 19:7), “all who sin under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom 2:12), “Speak and act as those who are going to be judged by the law that gives freedom” (Jas 2:12), “You sit here to judge me according to the law, yet you yourself violate the law” (Acts 23:3). How the law's judgment stands to the final judgment is a point the page does not take up here: the final judgment is on the judgment page.
rows._why: the words for judge, judgment, condemn, charge in the verse with the law, with the court scenes added by hand. The Hebrew שָׁפַט is 'judge' and 'govern'; the check reads whether the verse is a judgment about the law or only has a judge in it.

rows.label: Beside the covenant and the promise
rows.note: The verses that name the covenant or the promise beside the law, among them “They failed to keep God's covenant and refused to live by His law” (Ps 78:10), “the people have transgressed My covenant and rebelled against My law” (Hos 8:1), “The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God, so as to nullify the promise” (Gal 3:17) and “the promise to Abraham ... was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith” (Rom 4:13). These are different words in the Hebrew and the Greek (בְּרִית and διαθήκη covenant, ἐπαγγελία promise); the page says only that the verse names both, and takes no side on how the law and the promise stand to each other, which Christian traditions answer differently.
rows._why: review, 2026-10-25 (the scholar and the teacher): the first row was one 69-verse row whose label put the covenant and the promise first though only a dozen of its verses name either; split by the words in the verse, covenant half first, the Old Testament verses ahead of Gal 3 and Rom 4 in the Bible's order. A verse that names both a covenant and a commandment stands in both rows (match: all).

rows.label: Beside the testimony, statutes, ordinances (also “justice”, “righteous standard”), precepts and commandments
rows.note: The verses that name the testimony, the statutes, the ordinances, the precepts or the commandments beside the law, among them “because Abraham listened to My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws” (Gen 26:5), “the testimony of the LORD is trustworthy” (Ps 19:7), “Therefore the law is paralyzed, and justice never goes forth” (Hab 1:4), “so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom 8:4) and “the law is holy, and the commandment is holy” (Rom 7:12). These are different words in the Hebrew and the Greek (חֹק and חֻקָּה statute, מִצְוָה and ἐντολή commandment, עֵדוּת testimony, מִשְׁפָּט ordinance or justice, δικαίωμα righteous standard); the page says only that the verse names both.
rows._why: review, 2026-10-25: the second half of the split. The words for testimony, statute, ordinance, precept and commandment in the verse; the Berean prints 'justice' for מִשְׁפָּט in Hab 1:4, Isa 42:4 and 51:4 and 'righteous standard' for δικαίωμα in Rom 8:4, which the label now says.

rows.label: The law, and faith, believing

not_verses.Matt.23.23: πίστις here is 'faithfulness', one of the law's 'weightier matters' beside justice and mercy, not faith in God

rows.note: Set side by side with the next row, as the text has them: a verse that names both stands in both. In Rom 3:27 the Berean prints “principle” (“On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith”) where the Greek has νόμος; the original is kept and the row says so. Where Christian traditions part on how faith and the law stand to being made right with God, the page takes no side.
rows._why: πίστις or πιστεύω in the verse with νόμος (the Hebrew side has no verse that names both). Same rule as righteousness's 'Justified, and faith', whole verse and not clause.

rows.label: The law, and works
rows.note: “The works of the law” (Rom 3:20, 3:28; Gal 2:16, 3:2, 3:5, 3:10), the text's own phrase, kept as written. What “the works of the law” are, and how they stand to being made right with God, is a point on which Christian traditions part, and the page takes no side. Set beside the previous row: a verse that names both stands in both. In Rom 3:27 the Berean prints “principle” where the Greek has νόμος.
rows._why: ἔργον in the verse with νόμος. Hebrew מַעֲשֶׂה is left out: it stands in the law's verses only as 'work' in the Sabbath sense or 'the work of their hands'.

rows.label: The law, and grace

not_verses.Rom.7.25: χάρις here is 'thanks' ('Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!'), not grace

rows.note: “the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17) and “you are not under law, but under grace” (Rom 6:14) are in the text as written. Where Christian traditions part on whether grace replaces the law, completes it or stands beside it, the page takes no side.
rows._why: χάρις in the verse with νόμος.

rows.label: “Under the law”

not_verses.Rom.3.21: ὑπό here is 'by': the righteousness of God is 'attested by the Law and the Prophets'
not_verses.Heb.9.19: ὑπό here is 'by': the command was proclaimed 'by Moses'
not_verses.Jas.2.9: ὑπό here is 'by': 'convicted by the law as transgressors'

rows.note: The text's own phrase: “under the law” (Rom 6:14-15; 1 Cor 9:20; Gal 3:23, 4:4-5, 4:21, 5:18). Paul writes in 1 Cor 9:20 that to those under the law he became “like one under the law (though I myself am not under the law)”. Who is under it, and what it is to be under it, is a point on which Christian traditions part, and the page takes no side. In Rom 3:19 the Berean prints “those who are under the law”; the Greek there is ἐν (“in”) and not ὑπό, so that verse is not in this row and stands under “Every other use”.
rows._why: the preposition ὑπό next to νόμος (the very next word either side), so 'held in custody under the law' (Gal 3:23) but not a verse that only has 'by' and the law.

rows.label: Sin, trespass, the curse

not_verses.Amos.2.4: the people rejecting the law of the LORD: it stands in “Forsaken, rejected, forgotten, transgressed, not kept” and is not repeated here (review, 2026-10-25)
not_verses.Neh.9.29: the people's not obeying the law: it stands in “Forsaken, rejected, forgotten, transgressed, not kept” and is not repeated here (review, 2026-10-25)
not_verses.Lev.6.25: חַטָּאת here is 'sin offering' ('the law of the sin offering'), the offering and not sin
not_verses.Lev.7.7: חַטָּאת here is 'sin offering', the offering and not sin
not_verses.Lev.7.37: חַטָּאת here is 'sin offering' in a list of offerings, not sin
not_verses.Heb.10.8: ἁμαρτία here is 'sin offerings' in a list of sacrifices, not sin
not_verses.Acts.13.39: moved from the Greek's 13:38 (see moves): the 'sins' of 'forgiveness of sins' are printed in the Berean's 13:38, and this verse as shown has no word for sin

rows.note: The text's own words: “the law merely brings awareness of sin” (Rom 3:20), “where there is no law, there is no transgression” (Rom 4:15), “the power of sin is the law” (1 Cor 15:56), “Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice” (Deut 27:26), “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (Gal 3:10), “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Gal 3:13). Whether the law's curse is lifted, and for whom, Christian traditions answer differently, and the page takes no side.
rows._why: the words for sin, trespass, iniquity and curse (חַטָּאת, חָטָא, עָוֺן, פֶּשַׁע, אָרוּר, אָלָה, קְלָלָה, ἁμαρτία, παράβασις, κατάρα) in the verse with the law. The Hebrew חַטָּאת is also 'sin offering', which stands in Lev and Num verses of the row 'This is the law of ...' as well; the 16-verse check reads this.

rows.label: Other “laws” the text names: of sin and death, of the Spirit of life, of Christ, of freedom, of righteousness, the royal law, of marriage
rows.note: The text's own phrases: “another law at work in my body” (Rom 7:23), “the law of the Spirit of life set you free from the law of sin and death” (Rom 8:2), “the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2), “the perfect law of freedom” (Jas 1:25), “the royal law stated in Scripture” (Jas 2:8), “the law of marriage” (Rom 7:2), “Israel, who pursued a law of righteousness” (Rom 9:31). In Rom 3:27 (“a law of faith” in the Greek) and Rom 7:21 the Greek is νόμος and the Berean prints “principle” (“On what principle? On that of works? No, but on that of faith”; “So this is the principle I have discovered”): the verses are kept because the original has the word, and the page does not say which English is right. Whether these are the law of Moses under other names or other principles is a point on which Christian traditions part, and the page takes no side. Gal 6:2 names Christ in the verse; Rom 8:2 names “Christ Jesus”. “Under the law of Christ” in 1 Cor 9:21 is the Greek ἔννομος, a different word, and is named under the other words below.
rows._why: by hand (the phrases are not a word the builder can read): the verses where νόμος is qualified by another word. In Rom 3:27 and 7:21 MACULA glosses νόμος 'principle' and the Berean prints 'principle' too (sense_keep keeps them: the original arbitrates, and the row's note says so; found in the 16-verse check, which read the Berean text of Rom 7:21). Jas 1:25, 2:8 and 2:12 are included on the text's own phrases; Rom 7:2's 'law that binds her to her husband' and Heb 7:16's 'law of a fleshly commandment' are the other qualified uses.

rows.label: “Before the law was given”; “added because of transgressions”; “our guardian to lead us to Christ”; “only a shadow of the good things to come”
rows.note: The law in time, in the text's own words: “sin was in the world before the law was given” (Rom 5:13), “The law came in so that the trespass would increase” (Rom 5:20), “The law that came 430 years later” (Gal 3:17), “It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed to whom the promise referred” (Gal 3:19), “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ” (Gal 3:24), “the law is only a shadow of the good things to come” (Heb 10:1). This row and the two beside it are set side by side in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking. Where Christian traditions part on whether the law is fulfilled, ended, or continuing as a guide for the believer, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that put the law in time: before it, added, until, shadow, guardian. Gal 3:23-24 is in this row only; Rom 5:20 and Gal 3:19 are also in 'Sin, trespass, the curse'.

rows.label: Died to the law, released from it, not under it, redeemed from its curse; “Christ is the end of the law”; “abolished in His flesh”; “a change of law”
rows.note: The text's own words: “you also died to the law through the body of Christ” (Rom 7:4), “we have been released from the law” (Rom 7:6), “Christ is the end of the law” (Rom 10:4), “by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees” (Eph 2:15), “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law” (Gal 3:13), “when the priesthood is changed, the law must be changed as well” (Heb 7:12), “the law made nothing perfect” (Heb 7:19). In Rom 10:4 the Greek is τέλος, which means end, goal or completion; readers part on which Paul says, and the page does not choose. This row and the two beside it are set side by side in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking. Where Christian traditions part on whether the law is fulfilled, ended, or continuing as a guide for the believer, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that say a believer has died to the law, is released from it, is not under it, is redeemed from its curse, or that it ends, is abolished or changes. Rom 6:14-15 and Gal 5:18 are also in “Under the law”. Rom 7:1 ('the law has authority over a person only as long as he lives') was in the first build and is taken out: it states the premise and not the dying, which is Rom 7:4.

rows.label: “Not to abolish but to fulfill”; “we uphold the law”; not the least stroke will pass; summed up and fulfilled in love
rows.note: The text's own words: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets. I have not come to abolish them, but to fulfill them” (Matt 5:17), “until heaven and earth pass away, not a single jot, not a stroke of a pen, will disappear from the Law until everything is accomplished” (Matt 5:18), “Do we, then, nullify the law by this faith? Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law” (Rom 3:31), “so that the righteous standard of the law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom 8:4), “love is the fulfillment of the law” (Rom 13:10), “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (Gal 5:14), “in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2), “Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24:44). This row and the two beside it are set side by side in the alphabetical order of their labels and carry no ranking. Where Christian traditions part on whether the law is fulfilled, ended, or continuing as a guide for the believer, the page takes no side.
rows._why: by hand: the verses that say the law is fulfilled, upheld or not abolished, or that love sums it up. Matt 22:40 ('On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets') and Matt 7:12 ('this is the Law and the Prophets') are the Gospel's sums of the law, and are also in 'The Law and the Prophets'.

rows.label: Jesus speaks of the law: “I have not come to abolish”, “in your own Law”, “not one of you keeps it”
rows.note: The verses where Jesus Himself speaks of the law, in the Gospels' words. Luke 24:44 is the risen Jesus: “Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.” In John 8:17 and 10:34 He says “your own Law” and “your Law”, in John 15:25 “their Law”. The page says nothing here of what He meant beyond the words.
rows._why: by hand (the divine persons by hand, rule 4): each verse is Jesus speaking, or the Gospel quoting Him, with the word for law in it. Matt 22:36 (the lawyer's question) and Matt 22:40 (Jesus' answer) are the pair; only the answer is here.

rows.label: Every other use
rows.note: What no other row takes: the verses that name the law without saying what is done with it or how it stands to anything else, among them Deut 29:29, Neh 13:3 (“As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent”), Luke 2:27, Rom 7:1, 7:3 and 1 Cor 14:34, and four verses of Ps 119 (29, 51, 85 and 18).
